lessons.title: Cards before trading
lessons.question: At what price should trade happen?
lessons.text: The market is closed. Each buyer holds a card with the most they would pay: 9, 8, 7, down to 2. Each seller holds a card with their cost: 1, 2, 3, up to 8. On the board the blue staircase counts the buyers willing to buy at each price, and the red staircase counts the sellers willing to sell. Find where the curves cross.
lessons.explain: The staircases cross at p = 5. At that price five buyers want to buy and five sellers want to sell; the fifth pair, value 5 and cost 5, gains nothing. Trading every unit whose value exceeds its cost gives the largest total gain possible: 8 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 20. At any lower price buyers outnumber sellers, and at any higher price sellers outnumber buyers.
lessons.opens: Can traders who know nothing find that price?

lessons.title: Open the market
lessons.question: Can traders who know nothing find that price?
lessons.text: Open the market. Traders now shout random offers: a buyer bids any price up to their card, and a seller asks any price above their cost. When a bid meets an ask, the two trade at the price already on the table. Watch the price coin and the gold dots on the board until the period closes.
lessons.explain: These are zero-intelligence traders: no memory, no strategy, and no knowledge of the curves (Gode & Sunder 1993). Even so, a period usually ends with 4–5 trades at an average price near 5, capturing most of the possible gain. Over thousands of simulated periods the median is 95 % of the gain and the middle 80 % of period averages lie between 4.4 and 5.9. The double-auction rules, together with the ban on trading at a loss, do most of the work.
lessons.opens: Do the prices settle at the crossing?

lessons.title: Close to the crossing
lessons.question: Do the prices settle at the crossing?
lessons.text: Look closely at the board. Each gold dot is one trade, in order. Watch the next dots: early trades scatter, later ones close in on the dashed line where the curves cross.
lessons.explain: The first trade of a period typically lands about 0.7 away from 5 and the last about 0.05 away (medians over simulated periods). The traders with the highest values and lowest costs trade first, at scattered prices. As they leave, the remaining traders' ranges overlap only near 5, so later prices are squeezed towards the crossing. Smith (1962) saw human traders in the first classroom double auctions converge on the predicted price within a few periods.
lessons.opens: What happens when buyers get richer?

lessons.title: Buyers get richer
lessons.question: What happens when buyers get richer?
lessons.text: Give every buyer 2 more to spend. The blue staircase moves up, the crossing moves, and a new period starts. Watch the dots and the price coin until the period closes.
lessons.explain: Every value rose by 2, so the blue staircase moved up. The curves now cross at p = 6, where 6 units can trade instead of 5. The period's mean price (in the log) moves up with it, near 6 on average. A rise in demand raises both the equilibrium price and the quantity traded.

lessons.title: Costs rise
lessons.question: What happens when costs rise?
lessons.text: Now raise every seller's cost by 2. The red staircase moves up, and a new period starts. Watch where the dots and the price coin settle, and how many trades happen.
lessons.explain: The curves now cross at p = 7, with only 5 units worth trading. Prices rise again, averaging about 6.9 per period in simulation, but fewer units change hands. A fall in supply raises the price and lowers the quantity.
lessons.opens: Is it the traders or the rules that make the market work?

lessons.title: Drop the budget rule
lessons.question: Is it the traders or the rules that make the market work?
lessons.text: Switch the budget rule off. Traders may now bid above their card or ask below their cost, and so trade at a loss. Watch the dots and the price coin scatter, and read the share of the possible gains when the period closes.
lessons.explain: Without the rule every trader eventually trades, including buyers whose cards lie below the crossing and sellers whose costs lie above it. Their losses cancel most of the gains: here exactly 40 % remains (gain 8 of a possible 20, with these cards), and prices scatter around 6, the middle of the 0–12 range. The same random traders reach about 95 % with the rule on. As Gode & Sunder (1993) found, the constraint, a rule of the market, not the traders' intelligence, lifts efficiency close to 100 %.
